title: Working Time Rules
whatItIs: The Road Transport (Working Time) Regulations 2005 limit all the work you do, not just driving: 48 hours a week on average, 60 in any single week, plus breaks and night-work limits.

keyFacts.text: Weekly working time MUST NOT exceed an average of 48 hours over the reference period (17 or 26 weeks).

keyFacts: You can work up to 60 hours in a single week, as long as the 48-hour average is not exceeded.

keyFacts.text: You MUST NOT work more than 6 hours in a row without a break.

keyFacts: Working 6 to 9 hours: breaks of at least 30 minutes in total. Over 9 hours: at least 45 minutes.
Night work (00.00 to 04.00 for goods vehicles): no more than 10 hours of work in 24 hours.
There's no individual opt-out from the 48-hour average. Breaks and periods of availability aren't working time.

onTheTest.question: Your working day will total 8 hours. Under the working time rules, how much break must you take in total?
onTheTest.why: If working hours total between 6 and 9 hours, working time should be interrupted by breaks totalling at least 30 minutes. Over 9 hours: at least 45 minutes.

onTheTest.question: Under the Road Transport (Working Time) Regulations 2005, what is the most you can work in any single week?
onTheTest.why: A maximum of 60 hours can be worked in any single week, as long as the average of 48 hours a week over the reference period is not exceeded.

traps: Drivers' hours limit driving; working time limits all work, including loading and paperwork.
The 2005 rules have no opt-out. (Drivers under GB domestic rules can opt out of the 1998 48-hour average.)
Waiting only counts as availability if you know in advance how long it will last.
Working for two employers? You must tell each one, in writing, the hours worked for the other.
